<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-developed cases and answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 formatting. A's core mechanism (captivity enables price gouging and concentrated catastrophic risk; portability restores leverage and allows staged rather than big-bang replacement) was consistently defended and cleverly turned CON's own points back on it (e.g., reframing retraining cost as an argument against, not for, monolithic stacks; flipping "poor districts lack integrators" into "poor districts are most harmed by being locked to one integrator"). CON's case (integration prevents dangerous interaction failures, retraining dominates switching cost regardless of format, accountability diffuses under multi-vendor systems) was also strong and landed a genuinely sharp counter late in the debate — that A's "stable interface, swapped backend" fix could hide changed clinical logic and cause exactly the silent failures it claims to prevent. However, in the final exchange A identified a real structural tension in CON's fallback position: CON abandoned "one throat to choke" for a "rebid at renewal" leverage story, but that threat is only credible if the buyer can actually functionally switch — which is precisely what portability provides and lock-in denies. CON's closing response (vendors fear "losing everything" regardless of buyer switching cost) did not fully resolve this internal tension, whereas CON's own parallel point about hidden logic changes went unanswered by A's closing but was less structurally damaging to A's overall framework. On balance, A's rebuttal trajectory and closing move created slightly more decisive, unresolved pressure on CON's core mechanism than vice versa, though the debate was close throughout. A's opening was clipped for length, a minor execution cost, but it lost only a concluding rhetorical line rather than substantive content.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing (A5.1–A5.2), which exposed that CON's fallback leverage mechanism ("right to rebid the whole stack at renewal") is only credible if genuine portability exists, directly undercutting CON's claim that portability "adds nothing" to buyer leverage — a tension CON's closing did not fully resolve.</best_rebuttal>
